A YouTube recording titled “(88) ‘Prometheus Rising’ by Robert Anton Wilson - Chapter 7, with Alley Wurds @ VR Mystery School” features Alley Wurds, also known as Bubble, who says she has a bachelor’s degree in philosophy and has worked with and written about Prometheus Rising for five years.

In the Chapter 7 discussion, participants describe the first and second semantic circuits as evolutionary stable strategies based on negative feedback and homeostasis, while the third, time-binding semantic circuit is an evolutionarily unstable, revolutionary strategy based on positive feedback that seeks a new equilibrium at a higher energy level. They connect its upward spiral with progress and relatively open societies, while noting that taboos and dogmatism constrain it.

The discussion recounts Henry Adams’s attempt to describe accelerating social change mathematically by analogy with inverse-square laws, including his forecast of major energy leaps around 1900, 1917, and 1922; the speaker says his calculations were oversimplified. It also recounts Brooks Adams’s proposed stages of civilization—priestly control of knowledge, conquerors’ control of military power and government, landlords’ control of land, and national banks’ control of currency—and his observation that concentrated wealth shifted westward from Sumer through Egypt, Greece, Italy, Germany, London, and New York.

During the exercise discussion, participants said that observing people in opposing political echo chambers, including Black Lives Matter and reactionary groups, revealed how the same information can be interpreted to support opposing causes. One participant said seeing ancient-history and mystical ideas repurposed into ethnic-supremacist narratives was shocking; Alley Wurds emphasized empathy for people in extreme groups, including recognizing their fear even when their beliefs seem irrational.

A Lean Six Sigma failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) prioritized improvements to Intel’s R&D configuration-control process by risk priority number (RPN), using a cutoff to select process steps for improvement. Corrective actions aimed to simplify flow, reduce idle time and waste, and control output variation. The actions included removing redundant software approval by area experts (experts remained involved in writing the work package, or WP), which reduced the responsible R&D engineer’s waiting time by 35%; requiring technical and WP-quality feedback two days before review through configuration-control software, reducing idle time by about 9% of the WP cycle; shortening intervals between review forums, reducing non-value-added (NVA) time by 11%; assigning one technical-area contact to provide feedback, reducing NVA time by 4.5%; introducing WP quality-tracking sheets to assess clarity, technical content, risk assessment, evaluation plans, and implementation, with recognition for high scores and mentoring and manager notification for low scores; and standardizing WP templates, saving an estimated 0.5% of total WP-cycle time and reducing rework. Risk mitigation included organization-wide education and improved collaboration, delivered through relevant forums and a class for nano- and micro-scale manufacturing change-control WP authors and area experts. Overall, idle time per manufacturing change fell by 60%, exceeding the target, and standardization made the process more predictable and efficient without reducing technical rigor; company cost savings were not disclosed.

The R&D configuration-control changes from the Lean Six Sigma implementation were institutionalized through training materials, courses, and repeated sessions for stakeholders. First-time R&D work-package (WP) authors were required to take a class on the new process. Software tools integrated the corrective actions into a trackable system, and functional-area owners were assigned to support implementation and respond to system outages, making the changes sustainable without ongoing informal intervention. WP technical-content quality scores and average review times were monitored continuously using a quality-tracking sheet. The sheet was also intended to establish a measurable snapshot of the process’s current state at any future point, supporting further improvement.

The assistant described 50/50 as a typical songwriter–publisher royalty split, while noting that contract terms, the songwriter’s success, and the publisher’s role can alter it. The assistant gave illustrative examples: 60/40 with the publisher receiving the larger share for administrative services; 45/55 in the songwriter’s favor when publisher promotion or pitching generates income; and 30/70 with the publisher receiving the larger share when the songwriter has little bargaining power. These were presented as examples, not fixed industry rules.

The assistant said a songwriter may negotiate to take on administrative duties—such as registering works, licensing, and collecting royalties—in exchange for a larger share. It described self-publishing and co-publishing as possible arrangements, with terms and responsibilities negotiable; it also cautioned that administration takes time and can distract from creative work.

The assistant illustrated publisher promotion by pitching a songwriter’s pop song to a singer’s management, helping secure a recording, and obtaining a sync placement on a TV show. It said resulting exposure could lead to streaming and record-sale royalties, sync fees, and performance royalties from airplay; it gave 45/55 in the songwriter’s favor as a possible negotiated split when the publisher contributed significantly.

The assistant defined sync licensing as licensing music for visual media such as films, TV shows, advertisements, and video games. It said a sync use may generate an upfront fee and potentially further royalties; the sync fee might be split 50/50 or, in an illustrative case where the publisher secured the placement, 60/40 in the publisher’s favor. Additional income may include performance royalties and other royalties, split according to the parties’ agreement.

The assistant said well-known songwriters generally have greater bargaining power than lesser-known songwriters, potentially negotiating a higher share of royalties, larger advances, more copyright control, and better sync and revenue-sharing terms. It attributed this leverage to a track record and name recognition, while noting that a distinctive, in-demand songwriter may also negotiate better terms.

In response to the user’s question about improving bargaining power, the assistant suggested building a successful track record, developing relationships with multiple publishers, learning industry standards, hiring a music-industry lawyer or manager, or considering self-publishing. It noted that self-publishing can increase control over copyrights and revenue but brings greater administrative responsibility.
